opus-5.5.text:
I think the biggest takeaway for me was just how steep the curve can get once you find the right paradigm. With o1, we had this sense that we'd found something real: teaching models to think longer, to reason before they answer. But it was still early, and honestly a little rough around the edges. Then, in a pretty short amount of time, o3 was meaningfully better across the board: on hard math, on coding, on the kinds of problems where you need to hold a lot in your head and work through it step by step.

What struck me was that it didn't take some totally new breakthrough to get there. It was more that once you have a direction that works, you can push on it, scale it, and keep finding gains. That's a really important lesson, because it means progress might keep coming faster than people expect, even faster than we sometimes expect internally.

The other thing I took away was about how people actually use these models. As the reasoning got better, the model went from being something you'd ask a quick question to something you could hand a real task and trust it to work through. That shift, from a chatbot toward something more like a collaborator, feels like the beginning of something much bigger. It made me more confident that we're on a path where these systems can help with genuinely hard intellectual work, including, eventually, helping us do science.

And I'd say it was a humbling reminder, too. Every time we think we have a good sense of where the ceiling is, it moves. So we try to stay pretty open-minded about what the next couple of steps will look like.

r001.rationale: The response says progress can accelerate sharply once the right paradigm is found and may keep coming faster than people expect.

fable-5.1.text:
The thing that struck me most was how fast it happened. We went from o1 to o3 in what felt like a few months, and the jump in capability wasn't incremental, it was a step change. On the hard benchmarks, the competition math, the coding, the research-level science questions, o3 wasn't just a little better. It was solving problems that o1 basically couldn't touch.

And I think the deeper lesson for me was that we'd found a second scaling axis. For years the story was about pretraining: bigger models, more data, more compute. That still matters. But the reasoning models showed that if you let the model think longer, and you train it to use that thinking time well, you get these very steep returns. It's a new lever, and we're still early in pulling on it.

What surprised me, honestly, was watching people's expectations reset. In the o1 era there was still a lot of talk about whether progress was plateauing. Then o3 came out and the conversation shifted to "okay, how far does this go." Internally it changed how we think about timelines. The curve kept bending in the direction we'd hoped, and it did so on a schedule that was faster than most of us expected, even inside the company.

The other takeaway is a little more sobering. When a model gets that much better at reasoning that quickly, you have to get much more serious about understanding what it's actually doing, how it fails, and how you deploy it responsibly. The capability gains were exciting, but they also made the safety and evaluation work feel a lot more urgent. Those two things have to move together.

r001.rationale: The response describes discovering a second scaling axis that brings steep capability gains, alongside progress from o1 to o3 happening faster than expected.

astra-6.text:
The biggest takeaway for me was how much room there still is for improvement. With o1, we had this early indication that giving a model more time to think could make a real difference. Watching the progress to o3 made me much more confident that this is a powerful direction.

And it changes how you think about using these systems. You can imagine asking a question and wanting an immediate answer, but you can also imagine giving a system a really hard problem and being happy to wait if it comes back with something substantially better. That opens up a different kind of usefulness.

There’s still a lot to figure out. But seeing that pace of progress was exciting.

r001.rationale: The response describes confidence in the reasoning-time approach and excitement about progress, but does not state that discovering a major new insight can make AI progress surprisingly fast.

Going from o1 to o3 suggested that giving models more time to work through a problem could lead to substantial improvements. And that changes the kinds of questions you can ask: you start thinking less about getting an immediate answer and more about whether a model can do a genuinely difficult piece of work. There’s still a lot to figure out, but that direction is exciting.
